Valve needle seized from deposits or heat
Contaminated fluid or debris from a dirty pump filter

P208F.d: P208F is the Bank 2 version of P208E: the first dosing valve on the second exhaust branch fails to open although its drive circuit is in order. It only applies to engines with two separate SCR branches, each with its own dosing valve, which is rare; most diesel cars and trucks run one valve on Bank 1.
s: MIL and DEF or SCR warning
Higher NOx on one exhaust branch
Possible derate or countdown to no-restart
c: Urea crystals blocking the Bank 2 dosing valve
Valve needle stuck from deposits or overheating
Restricted supply line to the second valve

P2090.d: P2090 refers to actuator B, on engines with twin phasers the exhaust camshaft valve, on bank 1. What Low means depends on how the ECM drives the solenoid.
s: Engine warning lamp on, immediately on some GM V6 engines
Slightly higher consumption and emissions at part load
c: Exhaust valve control wire shorted to ground or engine block
Shorted coil in the exhaust oil control valve

P2091.d: P2091 says the control circuit of actuator B on bank 1, normally the exhaust phaser valve, sits too high. GM's high-side version on the 3.6 L LFX checks for a short to supply while the output is off and, like P2090, treats it as Type A after 20 of 25 samples; 18OBDG02 uses Type B.
s: Engine warning lamp on
Exhaust cam stays at default angle, slightly reduced performance
c: Exhaust valve control wire touching a supply wire
Incorrect splice or pin swap after earlier wiring repair
Failed output stage in the ECM

P2092.d: P2092 is the Low fault of the intake phaser valve (actuator A) on bank 2, which exists only on V and boxer engines with a separate valve per bank. Bank 2 is the side without cylinder 1.
s: Engine warning lamp on, immediately on GM LFX
Uneven running between banks, weaker torque
c: Bank 2 intake valve wire shorted to ground on the cylinder head
Shorted coil in the bank 2 intake oil control valve

P2093.d: P2093 reports too high a level on the control line of the bank 2 intake phaser valve (actuator A). Table 23OBDG07 shows why High and Low are not tied to one wiring fault: that GM controller switches the valve on the ground side, so it checks for voltage with the driver switched on and calls it a short to power after 1 s, with the lamp after two trips.
s: Engine warning lamp on
Bank 2 intake timing fixed, reduced low-speed torque
c: Bank 2 intake valve wire shorted to an ignition or injector feed
Fault in a shared engine harness connector

P2094.d: P2094 belongs to the fourth phaser valve of a twin-phaser V engine: actuator B, the exhaust camshaft, on bank 2. It is therefore absent on single-cam pushrod V8s and on inline engines.
s: Engine warning lamp on
Slight loss of efficiency, higher part-load emissions
c: Bank 2 exhaust valve wire shorted to ground
Shorted coil in the bank 2 exhaust oil control valve
Insulation damaged by heat near the exhaust manifold

P2095.d: P2095 closes the series: the bank 2 exhaust phaser valve (actuator B) shows a high level on its control line. For the 3.6 L LFX, GM table 19OBDG03B describes a high-side driver that finds a short to supply with the output off and sets a Type A code after 20 failures in 25 samples.
s: Engine warning lamp on
Exhaust cam on bank 2 fixed, minor drop in performance
c: Bank 2 exhaust valve wire shorted to a supply wire
Bridged pins in the valve or engine harness connector

P2096.d: Petrol engines run a slow outer control loop on the oxygen sensor behind the catalyst that shifts the mixture target of the front sensor. P2096 means this post-catalyst trim on bank 1 has hit its limit in the lean direction.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Usually no noticeable change in driveability
c: Rear oxygen sensor skewed rich, for example a contaminated reference air duct
Front sensor reading lean, so the engine actually runs rich
Calibration issue fixed by an ECM update
New catalyst not yet broken in

P2097.d: P2097 is the opposite limit of the post-catalyst trim on bank 1: the rear oxygen sensor keeps reporting lean exhaust, so the outer loop keeps adding fuel until it reaches its rich limit. GM's Bosch-based 2005 V6 sets it for a correction above +0.03 lambda; GM's 2018 four-cylinders list it as the high limit, with the integral offset at +99 % and total offset at +50 % or more (Type B); Ford's 2020 to 2023 engines set i
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Slightly higher fuel consumption
c: Exhaust leak ahead of the rear oxygen sensor drawing in air
Rear oxygen sensor skewed lean or aged
Calibration issue fixed by an ECM update

P2098.d: P2098 is the bank 2 version of P2096 on V and flat engines with a catalyst and rear oxygen sensor per bank. The post-catalyst trim of bank 2 has reached its lean-side limit because the rear sensor of that bank keeps reporting rich exhaust.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Usually no noticeable change in driveability
c: Bank 2 rear oxygen sensor skewed rich

P2099.d: P2099 is the bank 2 counterpart of P2097: the rear oxygen sensor of bank 2 keeps reporting lean exhaust, so the post-catalyst trim of that bank adds fuel until it reaches its rich-side limit. Ford sets it 5 s after the bank 2 rear bias trim reaches +0.087, with the closed loop running, coolant between 160 and 250 °F and at least 15 % fuel in the tank; GM's Bosch-based 2005 2.8 and 3.6 V6 and the 2008 3.6 LLT list it
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Slightly higher fuel consumption
c: Exhaust leak ahead of the bank 2 rear sensor
Bank 2 rear oxygen sensor skewed lean or aged

P209A.d: Air-assisted DEF dosing, as in Bosch's first Denoxtronic generation of 2004, mixes the fluid with compressed air before it reaches the exhaust, and a pressure sensor confirms that this air is there. A second sensor B can sit in another air branch or serve as a cross-check for sensor A.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp or SCR warning on
DEF dosing suspended, higher NOx output
Engine power derate or inducement countdown on trucks
c: Corroded or loose connector at sensor B, often from DEF residue or road spray
Reference voltage or ground of the sensor interrupted or out of range
Internal electronic failure of pressure sensor B
Input stage in the dosing control unit defective

P209B.d: Here the wiring of air pressure sensor B is intact and the voltage lies inside its valid band, yet the reported pressure makes no sense for the moment. Typical checks compare the value with the switching state of the air supply: pressure must rise when air is released to the mixing chamber and fall back when it is shut off, and with the system at rest it should sit near ambient.
s: Check engine or SCR warning lamp
Dosing reduced or stopped, possible NOx efficiency codes later
No noticeable change in driving until an inducement starts
c: Sensor B drifting or responding sluggishly
Leak in the atomizing air line between valve and dosing module
Sensing port blocked by urea crystals or dirt
Air supply valve sticking, so the expected pressure change does not occur

P209C.d: P209C means the signal of the second air pressure sensor in an air-assisted DEF system has dropped below the lowest voltage a working sensor can deliver. With common three-wire pressure sensors this points to a signal wire shorted to ground, a lost 5 V reference or a sensor failed internally; with some input circuits an open signal line also reads low.
s: MIL or SCR warning on
Live data shows pressure at or below zero regardless of air supply
DEF dosing switched off
c: Signal wire chafed through and touching ground
5 V sensor supply missing, for example pulled down by another sensor on the same rail

P209D.d: With P209D the second air pressure sensor reports a voltage above the top of its usable range, close to the supply or battery level. A real air pressure that high is not possible in the system, so the controller treats the value as an electrical fault.
s: Warning lamp on, dosing stopped
Displayed air pressure stays at an impossibly high value
Inducement countdown on heavy vehicles if not repaired
c: Sensor ground open at the connector or splice
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or battery voltage
Sensor B output stage failed high

P209E.d: When an air-assisted DEF system carries two air pressure sensors, the controller can compare them under conditions where both should read alike, for instance with the air supply shut and the lines vented to ambient, or at a steady dosing point. P209E is set when the two values stay apart by more than the calibrated margin even though each lies within its own electrical range.
s: SCR or engine warning lamp on
Live data shows clearly different values for sensors A and B at rest
Reduced or suspended DEF dosing
c: One of the two sensors drifted; compare both against a reference gauge
Restriction or crystal build-up in only one air branch
Leak in the air path between the two measuring points
Replacement sensor with a different pressure range fitted

P209F.d: DEF freezes at about minus 11 °C, so the tank is heated electrically or by engine coolant. P209F is not about a broken wire, which P202A to P202C report, but about the heating not behaving as expected: the tank does not warm up in the allowed time, or the heater or its valve runs too hot.
s: MIL and DEF system message, mostly in cold weather
Frozen DEF not thawed in time, dosing delayed after cold start
Speed limitation if the fault persists
c: Control unit software detecting a fault that is not there (FCA bulletins 18-091-16, 08-076-26)
Heater element partly degraded or poorly coupled to the fluid
Coolant heating valve sticking on coolant-heated tanks
Tank temperature sensor reading wrong, so heating looks ineffective

P20A0.d: After the engine stops, many airless DEF systems suck the fluid out of the line and injector back into the tank so that nothing freezes there. In Bosch's Denoxtronic 2.2 this is done by a 4/2-way valve in the supply module that reverses the flow.
s: MIL on (GM Type A, first trip)
DEF system or emission service message
Risk of frozen DEF line or injector in winter
c: Coil of the purge or reversing valve open
Connector at the supply module loose or corroded by DEF
Output stage in the engine or dosing control unit defective

P20A1.d: P20A1 judges the valve by its effect rather than its wiring. When the purge valve switches the pump into reverse, the pressure in the DEF line must drop.
s: MIL on after shutdown and restart
DEF warning message, possibly with other pump codes
Line not emptied, frost damage possible
c: Reversing valve in the supply module not shifting, often from crystallized DEF
Dosing control unit software detecting falsely (Hino SB-16-015)
Return or suction path blocked so pressure cannot drop
DEF pressure sensor reading wrong during the test

P20A2.d: The purge valve that reverses the DEF flow at shutdown is usually switched on the ground side. P20A2 reports that its control line is pulled too low, typically a short to ground somewhere between the driver and the coil, which would switch the valve on unintentionally or keep the driver from sensing it.
s: MIL on at once (GM Type A)
Service emission or DEF system message
Dosing possibly disabled
c: Control wire chafed against the frame or tank bracket
Moisture or DEF in the valve connector creating a leakage path
Valve coil shorted to its housing

P20A3.d: P20A3 is the high-side fault of the purge valve circuit: the line carries voltage or current where it should not. GM detects it on the 6.6 L Duramax while the low-side driver is switched on; an impedance of less than 0.5 Ω to controller power lasting 3 s triggers it as a Type A fault.
s: MIL on in the first trip (GM Type A)
DEF warning and possibly further pump codes
In frost, risk of DEF freezing in the line
c: Valve coil with shorted windings drawing excessive current
Control wire shorted to a battery-fed conductor
Damaged or DEF-contaminated connector bridging pins

P20A4.d: Stuck open means the purge valve stays in, or leaks into, its emptying position while the system is supposed to dose. Part of the pump output then flows back toward the tank, so working pressure builds slowly, collapses after the pump stops or needs a high pump duty to hold.
s: Warning lamp on, often with low DEF pressure codes
Slow pressure build-up after start
Higher NOx, possibly SCR efficiency codes
c: Worn or contaminated valve seat leaking internally in the supply module
Urea crystals holding the valve in the purge position
Valve energized permanently by a driver or wiring fault

P20A5.d: Stuck closed is the failure in which the purge valve does not switch to the reverse position when the system wants to empty the line. For the CNRB engine of the 2014 Touareg, Volkswagen bases P20A5 on the pressure difference between the start of the pressure reduction and the current value.
s: MIL on, often found after a shutdown cycle
No change in driveability (Ford software case)
Frost damage to line or injector if a real valve fault persists
c: Control module software (Ford 6.7 L, reprogram the glow dosing module)
Valve jammed in the delivery position by crystallized DEF
Return line to the tank kinked or blocked
DEF pressure sensor frozen at one value

P20A6.d: In an air-assisted DEF system the compressed air must reach the mixing point at a defined pressure, whether it comes from the vehicle's brake air supply or from a separate compressor. A solenoid valve sets or switches this air pressure.
s: SCR warning lamp or MIL on
Dosing stops for lack of atomizing air
Power derate on heavy vehicles
c: Solenoid coil of the air pressure control valve open
Connector unplugged or wire broken near the valve
Fuse or supply feed for the valve missing

P20A7.d: With P20A7 the air pressure control valve is electrically fine, but the air pressure it should produce does not appear. The check relies on the air pressure sensor: after the valve is opened or its duty changed, the measured value must reach the target band within a set time.
s: SCR warning, often together with air pressure codes
Poor atomization, possible deposits in the exhaust pipe
Rising NOx and later efficiency faults
c: Valve worn or contaminated with oil, water or urea deposits from the air supply
Insufficient supply pressure from the vehicle air system or compressor
Leaking air line or fitting downstream of the valve

P20A8.d: P20A8 says the air pressure control valve's drive circuit sits at too low a level, which normally means a short to ground. Depending on whether the valve is switched on the high or the low side, this either stops the valve from opening at all or energizes it without command.
s: MIL or SCR lamp on
Blown fuse possible on high-side switched valves
Dosing stopped, derate on trucks
c: Harness chafed through to ground along the frame
Solenoid coil shorted to the valve body
Water in the connector creating a path to ground

P20A9.d: If the control line of the air pressure control valve shows battery voltage or excessive current where it should not, P20A9 is stored. A wire touching a positive feed, a coil with shorted turns or a bridged connector can cause it.
s: Warning lamp on
Air pressure uncontrolled, often too high or permanently on
DEF dosing suspended
c: Coil with shorted turns causing overcurrent
Control wire shorted to a positive feed in the harness
Output stage in the dosing control unit defective

P20AA.d: P20AA describes a mechanical condition: the air pressure control valve lets air through even when it is commanded closed or to a lower setting. The air pressure sensor then shows pressure in phases where it should have fallen, for example after shutdown or during dosing pauses.
s: SCR warning lamp
Air pressure remains present with the valve commanded closed
Audible air flow at the dosing module, compressor runs more often
c: Debris, water or oil from the air system on the valve seat
Valve held open electrically by a wiring or driver fault

P20AB.d: The opposite of P20AA: the air pressure control valve does not open although the controller commands it, so no atomizing air reaches the DEF dosing point. The air pressure sensor stays near ambient during dosing requests.
s: MIL or SCR warning on
Air pressure stays at zero when dosing is requested
Power derate or inducement on trucks
c: Valve seized by corrosion or deposits
No supply pressure, for example low air reservoir or closed protection valve
Air line frozen with condensate or kinked

P20AC.d: P20AC is the general circuit code for the temperature sensor built into the reductant metering unit, meaning the DEF supply or dosing module that pressurises the fluid. The control unit typically relies on this value to judge whether the module has thawed and may start pumping.
s: Malfunction indicator or DEF/SCR warning lamp on
Dosing delayed or stopped in cold weather
Inducement countdown with speed or restart limit
c: Corroded or loose connector at the DEF supply/metering module
Damaged sensor wiring between module and control unit
Temperature sensor inside the metering unit failed (usually replaced with the module)
Input fault in the dosing or engine control unit

P20AD.d: P20AD covers a metering unit temperature reading that is electrically valid but does not make sense. A typical check compares it after a long cold soak with other temperatures that ought to agree, or watches whether it climbs once the module heater or warm coolant has had time to act.
s: Warning lamp after a cold start or longer drive
DEF dosing starts late or not at all in winter
Live data shows module temperature out of line with tank and coolant
c: Temperature sensor in the metering unit drifted (reads plausible but wrong)
Comparison sensor (DEF tank or coolant temperature) itself faulty
Contact resistance in the connector shifting the signal
Module heating or coolant heating not working, so the expected rise never comes

P20AE.d: P20AE is stored when the signal of the metering unit temperature sensor falls below its valid band. If the sensor is an NTC thermistor, the common design, though no maker confirms it publicly for this part, a low voltage stands for a very high indicated temperature.
s: Warning lamp on immediately after key-on
Module temperature shown far too hot in live data
DEF dosing suspended, inducement countdown possible
c: Signal wire shorted to ground (chafing near tank or frame)
Water or DEF residue bridging the connector pins
Sensor element in the metering unit shorted

P20AF.d: P20AF means the metering unit temperature signal has risen above its permitted band. For an NTC thermistor, the likely design though not publicly confirmed for this part, that looks like an extremely cold module.
s: Module temperature shown far below ambient in live data
DEF warning and delayed or missing dosing
Further SCR codes if the harness is corroded
c: Open signal or ground wire to the temperature sensor
DEF intrusion and corrosion in the pump connector or harness
Signal wire shorted to a supply voltage
Sensor element in the metering unit open

P20B0.d: P20B0 flags a metering unit temperature signal that jumps or drops out for brief moments instead of failing steadily. Housing, pump and fluid store a lot of heat, so the real temperature cannot change in leaps; the software treats such steps as a signal defect.
s: Warning lamp that comes and goes
Temperature value jumping in live data
Fault often not reproducible in the workshop
c: Loose or spread terminal in the module connector
Harness chafing intermittently against frame or tank bracket
Moisture entering the connector during wet or freezing conditions

P20B1.d: Many heavy-duty SCR systems thaw the DEF tank and supply module with engine coolant, and an electrically switched valve decides when that warm coolant may circulate; Bosch offers its larger supply modules with either electric or cooling-water heating. P20B1 is set when the control unit finds the drive circuit of this valve open or otherwise defective.
s: Malfunction indicator and SCR warning on
DEF thaws slowly or not at all in cold weather
Valve does not click during an actuator test
c: Valve connector unplugged, loose or corroded
Open solenoid coil in the coolant valve
Broken wire between control unit and valve

P20B2.d: P20B2 is a functional fault of the coolant valve that heats the reductant system: the circuit is intact, but temperatures do not follow the commanded valve position, most often because coolant keeps flowing while the valve should be shut. Hino uses the code in its dosing control unit and covers it in tech tip TT-16-014 for 2011–2017 conventional and 2013–2017 cab-over trucks.
s: Malfunction indicator with no other SCR fault stored
DEF tank temperature runs unusually high
Possible engine power restriction if left unrepaired
c: Wrong DEF tank or pump temperature input misleading the valve check
Coolant valve mechanically stuck open (deposits, debris)
Valve test blocked by other stored SCR faults, valve wrongly condemned

P20B3.d: P20B3 reports a low reading on the control line of the coolant valve that feeds the DEF heating, the classic picture of a control wire shorted to ground or a solenoid with shorted turns. Depending on how the output stage is wired, the valve then stays permanently energised or never responds, so the DEF can get too warm in summer or remain frozen in winter.
s: Malfunction indicator and SCR warning on
DEF tank overheats or does not thaw, depending on valve position
c: Valve control wire shorted to ground
Valve solenoid with shorted turns (low resistance)
Coolant or DEF inside the valve connector

P20B4.d: P20B4 is the opposite electrical case to P20B3: the drive circuit of the reductant heater coolant valve reads too high, which points to a short to battery voltage on the control line or, with certain driver designs, an interrupted ground return. The control unit can then no longer switch the valve, and the heating loop stays in whatever position the valve spring holds.
s: Malfunction indicator and SCR warning on
Valve cannot be actuated in an output test
Slow DEF thaw in winter
c: Valve control wire shorted to battery voltage
Open ground return of the valve circuit
Output stage in the control unit defective

P20B5.d: P20B5 concerns the electric heater inside the reductant metering unit, the element that keeps the pump module from freezing. The control unit sets it when this heater circuit is open or otherwise broken.
s: Warning lamp mainly in cold weather
DEF dosing starts late after a cold start
Inducement countdown possible
c: Heater element in the metering unit burnt out (usually module replacement)
Broken heater supply or ground wire
Corroded heater terminals at the module connector

P20B6.d: P20B6 is the functional check of the metering unit heater circuit: wiring and driver pass the electrical tests, yet the heating falls short of what the control unit expects, for instance the module temperature barely rises during a commanded heating phase or the current drifts away from its target. Such a monitor needs the heater to be running, so it can only reach a verdict in cold conditions and across a drive cycl
s: Warning lamp after cold starts only
Long delay before DEF dosing begins in frost
c: Aged heater element with reduced output
Metering unit temperature sensor reporting a wrong value
Low supply voltage to the heater (weak battery, poor ground)

P20B7.d: P20B7 means the metering unit heater circuit reads low. Volkswagen gives this a concrete meaning for the 2014 Touareg CNRB: the control unit checks heater conductance at the start of heating and flags P20B7 below 0.33 siemens, so the element shows more than about 3 ohms; further stages at 0.18 and 0.04 siemens follow.
s: Warning lamp at the start of a cold-weather heating phase
DEF dosing delayed in winter
c: Heater element resistance too high (aged or partly damaged)
Contact resistance at the heater terminals
Heater wire partly broken (few strands left)

P20B8.d: P20B8 marks the upper limit of the metering unit heater circuit. The 2014 Touareg CNRB table from Volkswagen sets it when the conductance measured at heating start exceeds 0.74 siemens, meaning the element is below about 1.35 ohms, with additional limits at 0.96 and 0.52 siemens.
s: Warning lamp as soon as heating is requested
Heater switched off, DEF stays frozen longer
Possibly a blown heater fuse
c: Heater element internally shorted (too low resistance)
Heater wires chafed and touching each other
DEF or water bridging the heater terminals

P20B9.d: P20B9 flags an open or broken control circuit for reductant heater A, one of the electric elements that keep diesel exhaust fluid liquid in winter. Which element carries the letter A differs by maker: GM's 2025 DEF tables call it heater 1, the tank heater; Ford links the code to the pump/heater assembly in the tank, Deutz to the suction line heater.
s: Check engine light, often first noticed in cold weather
DEF dosing starts late or not at all after a cold start
DEF system warning followed by a countdown to a speed limit
c: Water or DEF residue inside the heater or tank harness connectors (Ford TSB 21-2336)
Heater A element burnt out, so resistance is far above specification
Broken supply or return wire between control module and heater
Heater output stage in the DEF or engine control module defective

P20BA.d: P20BA is the plausibility test for heater A: the circuit is intact, yet the current, resistance or power the element takes does not match the command. GM's 2025 DEF tables compute the resistance of heater 1, the tank heater, and fail it below 1.00 or above 1.80 ohms, or when power strays more than 45 W from the request, after 8 s as Type A; the 2018 tables use a 1.05–1.93 ohm window.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp with DEF system message
DEF tank stays cold or frozen in winter although the engine is warm
Possible speed limitation after the inducement countdown
c: Aged heater element whose resistance has drifted out of the allowed window
Corroded or loose heater terminals adding resistance under load
Control software setting the code without a defect (FCA 18-028-14 reflash)
DEF pump unable to build pressure because of swapped or blocked lines (Volvo/Mack KC-4)

P20BB.d: A low reading on the heater A control circuit usually means the output or its wire is grounded, or the element pulls far more current than it should. GM's 2025 DEF module checks heater 1 (tank heater 1) in both states: switched on, a low-side drain voltage above 0.45 V or a load current above 95 A counts; switched off, the high-side voltage sitting in a low band near 0.5–0.6 V.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp, possibly with a blown heater fuse
Message that speed will be reduced if the system is not serviced
No DEF heating, so dosing is delayed in frost
c: Heater A wire chafed through and touching ground
Internal short in the heater element, drawing excessive current
DEF control module calibration setting the code falsely (GM 22-NA-112)
Moisture bridging heater pins to ground in the connector

P20BC.d: P20BC means the heater A control circuit reads high: the wire or output has picked up battery voltage, so the element may run when it should be off or cannot be switched at all. GM's 2025 DEF tables spot this on heater 1 (tank heater 1) mostly in the off state, when the high-side voltage lies between roughly 2 and 4.3 V instead of near zero; Type A after a 2 s debounce.
s: Check engine light and DEF system warning
Heater may stay energized, risking overheating or a drained battery
Reduced power or speed limit once the inducement starts
c: Heater A control wire shorted to a battery-voltage circuit
DEF control unit software fault (FCA 08-076-26 for 2025 Cummins Ram)
Heater output stage or relay stuck switched on

P20BD.d: Heater B's control circuit is open. In GM's tables heater 2 is the DEF line heater; the 2025 version detects the open state with the output off and sets a Type A code after two seconds, while the 2018 version relies on an open status reported by the DEF control module with battery voltage above 11 V.
s: Warning lamp, especially after cold nights
DEF pressure builds slowly or not at all in frost
Inducement countdown with eventual speed limit
c: Heating wire in the pressure line broken (line assembly replacement)
Corroded or unplugged line heater connector
Harness to the line heater damaged along the frame rail

P20BE.d: P20BE judges whether heater B, in most designs the heated pressure line, behaves as expected once the wiring itself checks out. GM's 2025 DEF tables flag line heater resistance below 2.80 or above 7.50 ohms, or a power error above 16.5 W, after 8 s (Type A); the 2018 tables accept a voltage-to-current ratio only between 1.51 and 3.57 ohms.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp after a heating phase
Ice in the pressure line on cold starts, dosing late
Possible NOx efficiency codes as a consequence
c: Pressure line heating wire degraded, resistance outside the window
High-resistance joint at the line heater connector
Engine control software setting the code erroneously (FCA 18-028-14)
Low heater supply voltage distorting the current measurement

P20BF.d: For heater B the code stands for a grounded control circuit or an overcurrent. Ford, where B is the pressure line heater, sets it when circuit 2 draws more than 15 A with the power stage on; the glow plug module can report such a short within 250 ms.
s: Check engine light, sometimes with a blown fuse
DEF pressure fault codes in cold weather
Speed limitation if the fault persists
c: Line heater wire chafed on the frame and grounded
Water in the line heater connector creating a path to ground
Internal short in the heated pressure line

P20C0.d: P20C0 reports that heater B's control circuit is high, typically a wire touching a battery feed or a driver that will not switch off. On Ford diesels B is the pressure line heater: with the power stage off, a current below 3 A while the output still carries over 5 V triggers it, and the glow plug module flags the condition in 250 ms.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp and DEF warning
Line heater may stay on with the engine off, draining the battery
Frozen pressure line once the module disables the heater
c: Line heater control wire shorted to a positive feed
Heater output stage in the DEF, engine or glow plug module stuck on
Bridged pins in a shared connector next to a supply terminal

P20C1.d: Heater C's control circuit is interrupted. Where the third element sits again depends on the maker: GM's 2025 DEF tables make heater 3 a second tank heater and test it like the others (output off, 2 s, Type A); Deutz assigns C to the return line heater; FCA's EcoDiesel has a heater 3 of its own.
s: Warning lamp mainly after cold soaks
DEF dosing delayed after a cold start
SCR warning and countdown if the fault persists
c: Heating circuit in the line or tank module open (resistance check at the connector)
Unplugged or corroded heater C connector
Glow plug control module fault where it drives the DEF heaters (GM LML)

P20C2.d: P20C2 says heater C is connected but does not take the power the control unit expects. In GM's 2025 tables heater 3, the second tank heater, must measure between 1.50 and 2.60 ohms and stay within 29 W of its command; otherwise Type A after 8 s.
s: Check engine light after a heating cycle
DEF thaws slowly in cold weather
Further heater codes if the common supply is weak
c: Heater supply below 5 V because of a weak relay, fuse or feed wire (Ford)
Engine control software setting the code falsely (FCA 18-028-14, 18-019-15)
Heater C element resistance outside its window

P20C3.d: A low C circuit points to heater C being grounded somewhere or drawing excessive current. GM's 2025 DEF module treats heater 3, its second tank heater, exactly like heaters 1 and 2: a low-band voltage with the output off, or drain voltage and current limits with it on, Type A once 2 s have elapsed.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp, possibly with no real fault present
Driver message that speed will be reduced without service
Unheated tank or line section in frost
c: Outdated DEF control module calibration on 2020–2022 GM diesel pickups (22-NA-112)
Heater C wire grounded through chafing
Shorted heater C element drawing overcurrent

P20C4.d: P20C4 marks heater C's control circuit as high, meaning it sees battery voltage where none belongs. GM's 2025 tables test heater 3, a second tank heater, with the output switched off against a raised voltage window and set a Type A fault after 2 s of persistence.
s: Check engine light and SCR warning
Battery drained overnight if the heater stays powered
Inducement and speed limit if left unrepaired
c: Heater C control wire in contact with a battery feed
Heater driver in the DEF or glow plug module stuck on
DEF crystals or moisture bridging pins in the heater connector

P20C5.d: P20C5 covers an open control circuit in reductant heater D, the fourth heating element that only a few SCR layouts carry. Deutz is the one maker found that publishes the code: in its EMR5/MD1 fault list D is the downstream line heater, and P20C5 maps to SPN 520471 with FMI 5, an open or too little current.
s: Warning lamp in cold weather
Dosing delayed while the downstream line thaws
c: Heating wire in the downstream DEF line burnt out or broken
Loose or corroded heater D connector
Wire break in the harness to heater D

P20C6.d: P20C6 is the functional check of heater D. FCA documents it for the 3.0 L EcoDiesel under the name Reductant Heater 4 Control Circuit Performance: bulletin 18-068-20 reflashed 2017 Ram 1500 engine computers that showed it, and a 2021 STAR case for 2020–2021 Ram 1500, Wrangler and Gladiator notes that it turns up mostly in severe cold, often without a defect.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp, mostly after very cold nights
DEF system message, sometimes alongside pressure codes
Often no noticeable change in how the vehicle drives
c: False detection in extreme cold with a still-frozen tank (FCA STAR S2118000006)
Leaking or blocked DEF supply line to the injector
DEF pump unable to build pressure or injector delivering the wrong quantity

P20C7.d: P20C7 reports that heater D's control circuit is grounded or overloaded with current. Only Deutz publishes the code: for its downstream line heater (SPN 520471) it maps to FMI 4, a voltage that is too low or a short to a low source.
s: Warning lamp, possibly with a blown fuse
Unheated downstream line and delayed dosing in frost
c: Heater D wire chafed through to ground
Water in the heater D connector
Internal short inside the heated downstream line

P20C8.d: Diesel exhaust fluid freezes at about -11 °C, so SCR systems carry several electric heating elements in the tank, pump and lines; which one a maker calls heater D varies. P20C8 reports that the control circuit of heater D reads high, meaning the output or its wiring has contact with battery voltage and the element can no longer be switched as commanded.
s: Check engine light and DEF or emission system warning
DEF dosing unavailable in cold weather, NOx warning or later speed limitation
Blown fuses and further unrelated codes when a chafed harness is the cause
c: Chafed harness letting the heater D control wire touch a battery-voltage feed
Moisture or DEF residue in the heater connector bridging pins
Internal short inside heater D or its integrated pump or line assembly
Faulty heater output stage in the engine or DEF control module

P20C9.d: P20C9 is a forwarding code. Some diesel trucks use a separate DEF or SCR control module with its own fault memory; when that module detects an emission-relevant fault it asks the engine module to switch on the check engine lamp, and the engine module records P20C9.
s: Check engine light with only P20C9 visible on a generic scan tool
DEF or SCR warning lamp, depending on the underlying fault
Possible power derate if the underlying SCR fault triggers inducement
c: Emission-relevant SCR fault stored in the DEF control module (heater, pump, pressure, sensor)
Failed upstream NOx sensor reported by the DEF module
Outdated or mismatched software between engine and DEF control module

P20CA.d: Air-assisted dosing, used mainly on older heavy and medium-duty diesels, mixes diesel exhaust fluid with compressed air from the vehicle's air system and blows the mixture through a nozzle into the exhaust. Airless pump systems in passenger cars and most current light trucks, such as Bosch Denoxtronic 2.2, have no air branch and cannot set this code.
s: Check engine light and SCR warning
Audible hissing near the dosing unit or air lines
Poor DEF atomisation, higher NOx and later engine derate
c: Leaking air hose or fitting between air supply and dosing unit
Worn seal on the air shut-off or pressure control valve
Leak in the vehicle's compressed-air supply feeding the doser
Cracked or poorly sealed dosing unit housing on the air side

P20CB.d: The engine computer checks the drive line of the hydrocarbon doser, a separate valve that sprays diesel into the exhaust ahead of the oxidation catalyst so the particulate filter can be heated for regeneration. This code means an open circuit: GM's diesel tables 18OBDG04 and 25OBDG04A watch the voltage on the switched-off driver output and flag a reading stuck in a mid band of roughly 2 to 3 V (Type B, MIL after two
s: Check engine light on
Particulate filter regeneration does not start or is aborted
Soot load warning and, later, reduced engine power
c: Corroded or loose connector at the doser, which sits under the vehicle in the exhaust area
Heat- or chafe-damaged wire between engine computer and doser
Open solenoid winding inside the doser
Faulty output stage in the engine control module

P20CC.d: Unlike the circuit codes, this one judges what the hydrocarbon doser actually does. On the 6.6 L Duramax LML/LGH, GM table 15OBDG09 sets it when the outlet of the oxidation catalyst runs more than 300 °C hotter than its inlet for 180 s although no regeneration is under way and more than 900 s have passed since the last one; that heat can only come from fuel the doser should not be delivering.
s: Check engine light on
Unexpectedly high exhaust temperatures, possibly white smoke or fuel smell
Higher fuel consumption
c: Doser leaking or dribbling fuel into the exhaust while closed
Coked nozzle tip with distorted spray
Exhaust temperature sensor before or after the catalyst reading wrong

P20CD.d: Here the control line of the hydrocarbon doser has a short to ground. GM's diesel tables 18OBDG04 and 25OBDG04A test the output while the driver is off: if the voltage drops below about 2 V, the line is touching ground.
s: Check engine light on after a single trip
Doser disabled, no active regeneration
Possible fuel smell or smoke from the exhaust
c: Control wire chafed through against the frame or exhaust
Water or salt in the doser connector bridging to ground
Internal short in the doser solenoid

P20CE.d: The control line of the hydrocarbon doser is shorted to battery voltage. GM's diesel tables 18OBDG04 and 25OBDG04A detect it while the driver is switched on: current above roughly 8 to 11 A for a set time, or above about 16 to 22 A at once, counts as a short to power.
s: Check engine light on
Active regeneration not possible
Rising soot load, later reduced power
c: Control wire touching a powered wire in a damaged harness
Doser solenoid with shorted turns drawing too much current
Faulty output stage in the engine control module

P20CF.d: The doser that adds diesel to the exhaust for filter regeneration is judged to stay open, so fuel keeps flowing after the command to close. On Volvo and Mack trucks the nozzle sits right at the turbo outlet and is fed by an AHI module; their troubleshooting guide KC-2157 points first to the fuel supply and then to that module.
s: Check engine light on
White smoke or strong fuel smell from the exhaust
Very high temperatures at catalyst and filter
Higher fuel consumption
c: Dirt or deposits holding the doser valve off its seat
Upstream shutoff or dosing module letting fuel through
Calibration error, fixed by a software update

P20D0.d: The exhaust fuel doser is commanded to inject but no fuel gets through, typically because the nozzle tip is plugged. Detection usually relies on line pressure that fails to drop or on too little heat build-up across the oxidation catalyst.
s: Check engine light on
Regenerations fail or are requested constantly
Soot warning and reduced power
c: Dosing module or supply valve not passing fuel
Kinked or blocked fuel line to the nozzle

P20D1.d: Injector B is a second exhaust fuel doser, found only on layouts with two dosing points, for example twin exhaust paths. This code reports a broken control line or open coil on that second unit.
s: Check engine light on
Regeneration incomplete on the affected exhaust path
c: Loose or corroded connector at doser B
Open solenoid winding in doser B

P20D2.d: With its wiring intact, the second exhaust fuel doser (B) is not delivering what was asked for: too little heat appears across the catalyst during dosing, or heat appears when it should be idle. No manufacturer documents P20D2 publicly.
s: Check engine light on
Longer or more frequent regenerations
Higher fuel consumption
c: Partly coked nozzle on doser B
Low or unstable fuel pressure feeding doser B

P20D3.d: The control line of the second exhaust fuel doser (B) is pulled toward ground. No manufacturer documents P20D3 publicly.
s: Check engine light on
Doser B switched off, regeneration impaired
c: Chafed control wire to doser B touching ground
Moisture in the doser B connector

P20D4.d: On the second exhaust fuel doser (B), the control line sits at or near battery voltage, so the driver cannot pull it low to open the valve. No manufacturer documents P20D4 publicly.
s: Check engine light on
Regeneration impaired, soot load rising
c: Control wire to doser B shorted to a powered circuit
Shorted turns in the doser B solenoid
Faulty output stage in the control module

P20D5.d: The second exhaust fuel doser (B) keeps passing fuel after it has been told to shut. No manufacturer documents P20D5 publicly; for the single doser A, Volvo and Mack trace the equivalent code P20CF to the fuel supply or the dosing module, and Ram fixed it on Cummins pickups with software.
s: Check engine light on
White smoke or fuel smell
Higher fuel consumption
c: Deposits keeping doser B from sealing
Upstream shutoff valve leaking fuel through
Calibration error in the control software

P20D6.d: The second exhaust fuel doser (B) fails to deliver fuel even though the control unit commands it open. No manufacturer documents P20D6 publicly.
s: Check engine light on
Failed or frequent regenerations
Reduced power once the filter is heavily loaded
c: Clogged nozzle tip on doser B
No fuel reaching doser B because of a blocked line or closed supply valve
Mechanically seized valve in doser B

P20D7.d: Upstream of the exhaust doser sits a valve that releases fuel to it only when a regeneration is wanted, often called the shutoff or fuel cut valve. This code reports an open in its control circuit.
s: Check engine light on
Active regeneration not possible
Soot warning, later reduced power
c: Loose or corroded connector at the dosing module
Broken wire in the dosing module harness
Open coil in the fuel shutoff valve

P20D8.d: The supply valve ahead of the exhaust doser is electrically sound, but the pressure it produces in the feed line does not follow its commands. A typical layout, described in a patent assigned to International Engine, measures that line pressure and uses it both to meter the dose and to diagnose the regulating valve.
s: Check engine light on
Regenerations take longer or fail
c: Low feed pressure from a clogged fuel filter or weak low-pressure pump

P20D9.d: For the fuel supply valve feeding the exhaust doser, the control line reads too low, which points to a short to ground. Volvo and Mack store P20D900 and, in AHI troubleshooting guide KC-2157, group it with the other electrical faults of the AHI module: check the module's connector and wiring harness.
s: Check engine light on
Dosing disabled, no active regeneration
c: Chafed wire in the dosing module harness touching ground
Water in the dosing module connector
Internal short in the supply valve coil

P20DA.d: For the supply valve ahead of the exhaust doser, the control line reads too high, typically because it touches battery voltage or, on some drivers, an open line pulled up internally. Volvo and Mack log it as P20DA00 and list it in guide KC-2157 among the AHI module electrical faults, with the instruction to check that module's wiring and connector.
s: Check engine light on
Active regeneration not possible
c: Valve control wire shorted to a powered line
Damaged coil in the supply valve
Faulty output stage in the control module

P20DB.d: The supply valve that should isolate the exhaust doser from the fuel system stays open after being switched off, so the feed line remains pressurized when no regeneration is running. If the doser itself then leaks, fuel can reach the hot exhaust unasked.
s: Check engine light on
Fuel smell or smoke if the doser also leaks
Long cranking after fuel system work
c: Supply or fuel cut valve sticking open from wear or dirt
Detection or control calibration error, fixed by software
Contaminated fuel leaving deposits in the valve

P20DC.d: The valve feeding the exhaust doser does not open when a regeneration starts, so the doser receives no fuel. A Hino patent shows how this is recognized: a pressure sensor between the shutoff valve and the dosing valve reads far below a threshold that depends on engine speed.
s: Check engine light on
Regenerations fail, soot load keeps rising
Reduced power in later stages
c: Clogged fuel filter or water and dirt in the fuel
Internal fault in the dosing module

P20DD.d: The pressure sensor in the feed line of the exhaust doser lets the control unit meter fuel and spot a stuck valve or plugged nozzle. This code is the general circuit fault of that sensor; signal too low, too high and unsteady have their own codes (P20DF, P20E0, P20E1).
s: Check engine light on
Active regeneration blocked
Further codes for the reference voltage or the dosing system
c: Internally damaged harness to the dosing module and its sensor

P20DE.d: The doser feed pressure sensor gives a signal inside its electrical limits, yet the value does not fit what the system is doing, for example no pressure rise when the supply valve opens. Hino uses the code widely: SB-18-029 (2017–2019 J08 and J05 trucks, MIL on) has a specific sensor batch replaced, earlier notes blame a fuel cut valve that hangs or dirty fuel clogging a filter, and SB-22-007 swaps a 2020 bubbler fil
s: Check engine light on
Regeneration interrupted or blocked
Sometimes further fuel pressure codes such as P0087
c: Restricted fuel or separator filter from contaminated fuel
Sticking fuel cut or supply valve
Plugged nozzle or leaking fuel/air line

P20DF.d: The signal of the doser feed pressure sensor sits below its lower limit. Electrically that suggests a grounded signal line or a missing reference voltage.
s: Check engine light on
Regeneration blocked
c: Real low pressure from a restricted filter or contaminated fuel
Signal wire shorted to ground or reference voltage lost
Outdated detection threshold, fixed by a software update

P20E0.d: The doser feed pressure sensor reports a signal above its upper electrical limit. On a typical three-wire sensor this happens when the signal line is open and pulled up, shorted to the 5 V reference or to battery voltage, or when the ground is lost.
s: Check engine light on
Active regeneration blocked
c: Signal wire open or shorted to reference or battery voltage
Sensor from a faulty production batch

P20E1.d: The signal from the pressure sensor in the doser feed line jumps or drops out for short moments, faster than real line pressure could change. Usual reasons are a loose pin, a cracked wire flexing with engine movement, or moisture in the connector.
s: Check engine light on, possibly coming and going
Regenerations interrupted
c: Loose or fretted pins at the sensor connector
Internal fault in the pressure sensor

P20E2.d: P20E2 flags that bank 1 exhaust temperature sensors 1 and 2 disagree at a moment when both should show nearly the same value. Sensor 1 usually sits ahead of the oxidation catalyst and sensor 2 behind it.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on, often with no change in driving
Particulate filter regeneration delayed or blocked
Code returns after a long parking period
c: Exhaust temperature sensor 1 or 2 drifted or aged (offset reading)
Corroded or loose connector adding resistance to one sensor signal
Sensors swapped or a non-matching replacement part installed
Engine control software needing an update

P20E3.d: P20E3 reports that exhaust temperature sensors 1 and 3 on bank 1 do not agree. In the usual diesel order, sensor 1 measures before the oxidation catalyst and sensor 3 after the particulate filter, so this pair brackets the whole aftertreatment line.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Particulate filter regeneration postponed
Temperature values of sensors 1 and 3 differ noticeably on a cold engine
c: Sensor 1 or sensor 3 reading offset or responding sluggishly
Water or corrosion in the connector of the rear sensor
Exhaust leak near one sensor letting outside air cool its tip

P20E4.d: P20E4 covers the pair around the particulate filter: sensor 2 at the filter inlet and sensor 3 at its outlet on bank 1 no longer agree. GM documents the code for the diesel in table 15OBDG04 (also 14OBDG04): after a soak of at least 28,800 s the start-up values of the filter upstream and downstream sensors are compared against a look-up limit, and a larger gap is a Type B fault.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Regenerations aborted or happening more often
Filter loading warning in some vehicles
c: Filter inlet or outlet temperature sensor aged by heat cycling
Heat-damaged or corroded sensor connector or lead
Heavy soot or ash deposits on a sensor tip slowing its response

P20E5.d: P20E5 is the bank 2 counterpart of P20E2: on engines with a separate exhaust and aftertreatment path per cylinder bank, sensors 1 and 2 of the second bank disagree after the system has cooled down. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; the GM tables that use P20E2 cover single-path diesels.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Bank 2 sensors show different values on a cold engine
c: Contact resistance in a bank 2 sensor connector
Sensor connectors swapped between banks after a repair

P20E6.d: This code belongs to air-assisted DEF dosing, where compressed air carries the fluid to the nozzle and breaks it into fine droplets; airless pump systems in cars and most current pickups do not use it. P20E6 means the air pressure in the dosing branch stays below the minimum the control unit needs while dosing is requested.
s: Check engine light and SCR warning
DEF dosing reduced or stopped, rising NOx emissions
Engine derate after the inducement period
c: Insufficient air tank pressure from a leak or weak compressor
Air shut-off or pressure control valve not opening
DEF crystals restricting the air side of the dosing unit
Leaking, kinked or blocked air line to the doser

P20E7.d: On air-assisted DEF dosing the control unit regulates the compressed air fed into the mixing chamber so that the nozzle sprays a stable mist. P20E7 is set when the measured air pressure climbs above the permitted upper limit, for instance because the pressure control valve no longer throttles and passes full tank pressure, or because the path downstream of the sensor is narrowed so pressure builds up in front of it.
s: Check engine light and SCR warning
Irregular DEF spray, deposits in the exhaust and higher NOx
Engine derate if dosing is shut down
c: Air pressure control valve no longer regulating and passing full supply pressure
DEF crystals or deposits restricting the nozzle or mixing path
Air pressure sensor reading too high

P20E8.d: Airless DEF systems hold the fluid at a set pressure ahead of the dosing valve with an electric pump, read by a pressure sensor. P20E8 means the measured value stays clearly below that target or cannot be built up at all.
s: Check engine light and DEF system warning message
No DEF dosing, rising NOx and a countdown to speed limitation or no restart
Pump can be heard running longer than usual after key on
c: Air in the DEF lines or pump that lost its prime, for example after long storage
Clogged pump inlet, suction tube, filter or tank vent, often from contamination
External leak at a DEF line, connector or the dosing valve
Worn, crystallised or superseded DEF pump unit

P20E9.d: P20E9 is the overpressure counterpart of P20E8: during closed-loop control the DEF pressure ahead of the dosing valve rises clearly above its target. Ford's 2023 diesel summary sets it at more than 150 kPa over setpoint; GM's 18OBDG04 table asks for the same 150 kPa excess while the pump runs below 3,200 rpm (Type A), and GM's 2025 DEF table 25OBDG04A uses a 63 kPa window for 4 s.
s: Check engine light and DEF system warning
Dosing shut off, NOx warning and later inducement countdown
c: Blocked return path, restricted line or dosing valve not opening properly
Debris in the fluid after a damaged filter seal or dirty refilling
Reductant pressure sensor reading too high
Pump control software needing an update

P20EA.d: Many SCR systems supply the reductant control module, and through it pump and heaters, via a power relay. After the key is switched off the relay should stay energised for a short after-run so the pump can empty the lines and the module can save its learned values, and only then drop out on the module's command.
s: Check engine light, often without noticeable driving symptoms
DEF lines not purged, risk of frozen or crystallised lines in winter
c: Worn relay contacts or coil interrupting the supply early
Loose fuse, terminal or ground in the relay or module feed
Battery disconnected or voltage collapsing right after shut-off
Reductant control module releasing the relay prematurely

P20EB.d: Here the opposite of P20EA happens: after the reductant control module has finished its after-run and released the power relay, voltage is still present on the switched side, so the relay opens late or not at all. Typical reasons are welded contacts, a control line shorted to ground that keeps the coil energised, or a module that never ends its shut-down.
s: Check engine light
Battery drained after the vehicle has been parked
DEF pump or relay audible long after switching off
c: Relay control line shorted to ground, keeping the coil energised
Reductant control module or network activity preventing shut-down

P20EC.d: P20EC means the engine computer has registered a temperature in the SCR catalyst of bank 1 above the limit its washcoat can tolerate. The limit depends on the formulation: vanadium-based SCR material starts to sublimate irreversibly above roughly 550 °C, as Navistar's patent US20190232224 and the US rule 40 CFR 1036.115 both state, and US heavy-duty certification requires engine makers to protect such catalysts from
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Regeneration interrupted or power reduced to protect the aftertreatment
Later loss of NOx conversion (follow-up code P20EE)
c: Excess heat release during particulate filter regeneration
Unburnt fuel or oil reaching the exhaust (leaking injector, turbo seal)
SCR temperature sensor reading too high
Regeneration or thermal-management calibration needing an update

P20ED.d: P20ED applies to systems with two SCR stages in series: a small pre-catalyst mounted close to the engine, often with its own dosing unit, ahead of the main SCR brick. The code says this front stage on bank 1 got hotter than permitted.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Front SCR dosing stopped or regeneration interrupted
Higher NOx emissions after a cold start
c: Heat from oxidation catalyst or filter regeneration reaching the close-coupled stage
Fuel or oil entering the exhaust upstream of the pre-catalyst
Temperature sensor at the pre-catalyst reading too high

P20EE.d: P20EE is the main monitor CARB requires for the NOx-reducing catalyst: the share of NOx removed by the SCR catalyst on bank 1, judged by the NOx sensors before and after it, has fallen below what the system needs. Ford's 2023 6.7 L diesel fails it when cumulative efficiency drops under 55 % with the SCR inlet at 200–320 °C.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
DEF or exhaust fluid quality warning in the instrument cluster
Speed limitation countdown on some vehicles if the fault persists
c: Diluted or contaminated DEF, or a clogged or leaking dosing valve
Upstream or downstream NOx sensor reading wrong
SCR catalyst aged, overheated or poisoned
Exhaust leak between the two NOx sensors
Calibration needing an update (several manufacturer bulletins)

P20EF.d: P20EF concerns the front stage of an SCR arrangement with two stages on bank 1: the pre-catalyst no longer removes enough NOx. CARB allows catalysts in series to be monitored individually or together; this code is used where the front stage is checked separately, which requires a NOx sensor between the two bricks.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Higher NOx at low exhaust temperatures, for example after cold starts
c: Front DEF dosing valve clogged, crystallised or leaking
NOx sensor before or between the stages reading wrong

P20F0.d: P20F0 is the bank 2 version of P20EC: the SCR catalyst in the second exhaust line has been exposed to temperatures above its permitted limit. It presupposes a V engine with one aftertreatment path per bank, which is rare; most diesels merge both banks into one SCR line and use only the bank 1 codes.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Reduced power or interrupted regeneration to protect the catalyst
c: Leaking injector or misfire on bank 2 sending fuel into the exhaust
Excess heat during particulate filter regeneration on bank 2
Bank 2 SCR temperature sensor reading too high

P20F1.d: P20F1 reports an over-temperature of the SCR pre-catalyst on bank 2, the close-coupled front stage of a two-stage system in the second exhaust line. Both conditions must be met for the code to exist on a vehicle: separate aftertreatment per bank and a split SCR with a front brick near the turbocharger outlet.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Front-stage dosing or regeneration suspended
c: Fuel slip from bank 2 cylinders (injector leak, misfire, post-injection fault)
Pre-catalyst temperature sensor on bank 2 reading too high
Regeneration heat reaching the front stage

P20F2.d: P20F2 is the bank 2 twin of P20EE: the main SCR catalyst of the second exhaust line removes less NOx than required, judged by NOx sensors ahead of and behind it. CARB requires the NOx catalyst to be flagged once its conversion loss would push emissions past the regulatory multiple of the standard.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
DEF quality warning, possibly with a countdown to reduced speed
c: Poor DEF quality or bank 2 dosing valve fault
Bank 2 SCR catalyst aged or overheated
Exhaust leak between the bank 2 NOx sensors

P20F3.d: P20F3 states that the SCR pre-catalyst on bank 2 no longer converts enough NOx. It belongs to engines with a separate aftertreatment line per bank and a two-stage SCR in each, with a NOx sensor between front and main brick so that the front stage can be judged on its own, an option CARB grants for catalysts arranged in series.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Increased NOx after cold starts
c: Bank 2 front dosing valve blocked or crystallised
NOx sensor between the bank 2 stages reading wrong
Bank 2 pre-catalyst damaged by heat or contamination

P20F4.d: The control unit compares the DEF quantity it commands with what the system actually delivers, judged from tank level, pump effort or the long-term correction the NOx feedback needs. P20F4 means too little fluid is really reaching the exhaust.
s: Check engine light and DEF warning
DEF tank level falls slower than expected
Higher NOx emissions and, if unresolved, inducement countdown
c: Partly blocked or crystallised dosing valve delivering less than commanded
Air pockets in the injector line, as Mercedes reports for the OM654 Sprinter
Leak in tank, pump or line so less fluid reaches the valve
Dosing control unit software requiring an update

P20F5.d: P20F5 is set when more diesel exhaust fluid is used, or has to be corrected away, than the control unit planned. In VW's 2014 Touareg TDI data book the trigger is an SCR adaptation value of 0.51 or lower: the NOx feedback keeps cutting the commanded dose because more fluid evidently reaches the catalyst than intended.
s: Check engine light and DEF warning
DEF tank empties faster than usual, white crust around the dosing valve
Ammonia smell or deposits in the exhaust
c: Dosing valve dripping or not sealing between pulses
External leak at the valve or its supply line
Pressure sensor reading low, causing excess delivery
Dosing control unit software requiring an update

P20F6.d: Between pulses the dosing valve must seal tightly so DEF only enters the exhaust when commanded. P20F6 means the control unit concluded that the first valve on bank 1 stays open: the pressure collapses, or the pump has to work much harder to hold it than the commanded quantity explains.
s: Check engine light and DEF warning
Higher DEF consumption, white deposits in the exhaust or ammonia smell
Dosing switched off and later inducement
c: Crystals or debris on the valve seat keeping the valve from closing
Mechanically sticking or heat-damaged dosing valve
Control unit software misjudging valve closure, cured by an update
Leaking or detached line at the valve imitating an open valve

P20F7.d: P20F7 is the bank 2 version of P20F6 and only applies to engines with a second exhaust line that has its own SCR catalyst and dosing valve, typically V engines with separate aftertreatment per bank. The control unit judges that this valve no longer closes, usually because pressure cannot be held or the pump must deliver far more than the commanded dose.
s: Check engine light and DEF warning
Higher DEF consumption and deposits in the bank 2 exhaust
Dosing switched off and later inducement
c: Crystals or debris on the bank 2 valve seat
Mechanically sticking or heat-damaged bank 2 dosing valve
Leaking or detached supply line at the bank 2 valve

P20F8.d: P20F8 means the intake manifold runner or swirl flaps on bank 1 do not follow the commanded position, judged by comparing set point and feedback from the position sensor. Unlike P2004/P2006, which state a direction (stuck open or closed), this code reports poor tracking anywhere in the travel.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Rough idle or hesitation at low speed
Less torque at low engine speed
c: Flaps or shaft sticking from carbon and oil deposits (common on diesels with EGR)
Worn or overheating actuator motor or failed position sensor
Control software needing an update (Mazda bulletin 01-003/26)
Wiring or connector fault at the actuator

P20F9.d: P20F9 is the bank 2 counterpart of P20F8: the runner or swirl flaps of the second cylinder bank do not track their commanded position. It needs a V engine whose banks have separately driven flaps, each with its own position feedback.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Uneven idle or reduced torque at low speed
c: Bank 2 actuator or position sensor faulty
Broken or detached linkage between actuator and flap shaft

P20FA.d: P20FA means the controller has found an open or otherwise faulty drive circuit for the second reductant (DEF/AdBlue) pump, called pump B or pump 2. No public service text explains which physical pump carries this letter; it is a driver channel of its own, separate from pump A (P208A).
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Service DEF or AdBlue warning with countdown to restart lockout
Other SCR codes stored at the same time (P208A, P20FC, P20FD)
c: Water ingress or corrosion in the pump B connectors or harness
Connector not fully latched after assembly or repair
Open winding or internal break in pump B
Faulty output stage in the engine or DEF control module

P20FB.d: P20FB is the functional check of reductant pump B: its circuit is electrically sound, yet the pump does not reach the commanded state or stays off when it should be running. No public threshold exists for pump B.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
DEF system warning, possibly with countdown to restart lockout
Code returns mainly after cold starts or long parking
c: Outdated PCM software (FCA 3.0L EcoDiesel, reflash bulletins)
Pump B worn, seized or blocked by crystallised fluid
Frozen DEF or failed tank heating in cold weather
Clogged pump filter or restricted lines

P20FC.d: P20FC sets when the drive signal for reductant pump B reads too low, typically a ground fault on the line or a current draw beyond what the driver allows. Pump B has no published limits.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
DEF system warning and reduced or no reductant dosing
Restart lockout after the inducement countdown if left unrepaired
c: Chafed wire shorting the pump B control line to ground
Water ingress or corrosion in the pump connectors
Pump B motor drawing excessive current (internal short or tight motor)
Faulty output stage in the control module

P20FD.d: P20FD indicates that the control line of reductant pump B sits too high, for instance shorted to battery voltage, so the controller can no longer regulate the pump properly. No limits are published for pump B.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
DEF system warning, dosing suspended
Countdown to restart lockout in the instrument cluster
c: Pump B control line shorted to battery or supply voltage
Moisture or corrosion bridging pins in the pump connectors
Internal electrical fault in pump B
Faulty output stage in the control module

P20FE.d: P20FE judges whether the first reductant metering unit actually delivers the quantity the SCR control asks for. GM's 2025 Duramax tables average a delivery compensation factor and set the code, Type A after one trip, once that factor passes 1.44, meaning the expected pressure drop no longer proves correct dosing.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
AdBlue/DEF system warning in the cluster
Higher NOx, possible SCR efficiency codes (P20EE)
c: Partly blocked or crystallised dosing injector
Loose or damaged tank filter letting debris reach pump and sensor
Air in the dosing lines after service or low fluid level

P20FF.d: P20FF is an internal fault of the module that runs the DEF pump and heaters, not of the pump itself. Ford's 2023 6.7L diesel strategy sets it when the pump motor controller exceeds 130 °C or reports an internal error, detected within about 5 seconds as part of the pump function check.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Service DEF System message, on some GM trucks wrongly shown as DEF Low
DEF dosing stops and the inducement countdown may begin
c: Internal memory or processor fault in the DEF control module
Software or calibration mismatch after programming
Poor power or ground connection causing module resets
